results.title: GPU Cloud Pricing Explained: On-Demand, Reserved, Bare Metal
highlights:
# GPU Cloud Pricing Explained: On-Demand, Reserved, and Bare Metal

GPU cloud pricing is more than an hourly rate. This guide explains on-demand, reserved, and bare metal options, when each makes financial sense, and how utilization affects costs. Compare GMI Cloud GPU rates, break-even points, and hidden expenses to choose the right pricing model.

October 21, 2026

GPU cloud pricing looks simple on a rate card, but the hourly number hides two separate decisions: How you commit to paying for capacity, and how much of the server you actually get. Understanding both is what separates a GPU bill that tracks useful work from one that pays for idle hardware.

- On-demand buys flexibility: You pay per GPU-hour with no commitment and can stop at any time, which suits experiments, bursty jobs, and workloads whose utilization you have not measured yet.
- Reserved pricing buys a lower rate: Committing to a term lowers the effective hourly price, but you pay for every hour of the term, so it only saves money when utilization stays above the break-even point set by the discount.
- Bare metal is a deployment model, not a billing term: It gives you the whole physical server with root access and no hypervisor, which can be bought on demand or reserved, and NVIDIA has measured virtualized training running 12% slower than bare metal.
- Published rates are only a starting point: On GMI Cloud, on-demand rates start at $2.60 per GPU-hour for H100, $3.20 for H200, $5.00 for B200, and $8.00 for GB200 as of October 2026, while committed plans are discounted and storage and networking are priced separately.
- Utilization decides which model wins: Cast AI’s 2026 analysis of production clusters found average enterprise GPU utilization of roughly 5%, which shows how easily reserved capacity turns into paid idle time. Matching the pricing model to measured usage is the single biggest lever on GPU cost.

...

### How On-Demand Billing Works

On-demand pricing charges a rate per GPU-hour while your instance is running, with no minimum term. You can start, scale, and stop whenever you like, and the bill follows usage, provided you actually release capacity when it is idle. Metering granularity matters for short jobs. Some providers bill by the second or minute, others round up to the hour, and that difference adds up quickly for bursty work.

On GMI Cloud, all GPU resources are dedicated, single-tenant instances priced per GPU-hour, with the rate depending on GPU type and deployment model. Pay-as-you-go containers have no expiration date and can be terminated at any time, and pay-as-you-go managed clusters are charged by the minute with no upfront cost, as GMI explains in its guide to comparing container, bare metal, and managed cluster quotes.

### When On-Demand Is the Right Choice

On-demand pricing wins whenever the workload is short, bursty, or not yet measured. That covers prototyping, benchmarking a new model, one-off fine-tuning runs, evaluation jobs, and inference traffic whose daily pattern you have not seen yet. It is also the right way to start almost any new project, because a few weeks of on-demand usage turns a utilization guess into a measured number before you commit to anything.

### On-Demand GPU Rates on GMI Cloud

The table below shows GMI Cloud’s published starting rates, taken from the GMI Cloud pricing page in October 2026. Rates vary by region and deployment model and can change with promotions, so treat them as starting points and confirm the live rate in the GMI Cloud console before you budget.

| GPU | On-demand rate (October 2026) | Availability (October 2026) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| NVIDIA H100 | From $2.60 per GPU-hour | Available now |
| NVIDIA H200 | From $3.20 per GPU-hour | Available now |
| NVIDIA B200 | From $5.00 per GPU-hour | Limited availability |
| NVIDIA GB200 | From $8.00 per GPU-hour | Available now |
| NVIDIA GB300 | Pre-order | Pre-order |

...

On GMI Cloud, containers can run on prepaid plans with renewal periods from one day to three years, and a prepaid container cannot be terminated before its rental period ends. Committed usage plans are discounted relative to on-demand, with volume and custom pricing handled by the sales team. Before you confirm an order, the console shows the list price, the discount, and the estimated monthly total, which makes it easy to compare a committed plan with the on-demand equivalent.

...

The GPU-hour rate usually covers compute only. On GMI Cloud, storage and networking are priced separately when you allocate them, and several of these line items can outweigh a small difference in GPU rates. Persistent storage is one, since container-local data does not survive reconfiguration and workloads that need durable data need a volume. Public IP addresses are another. GMI Cloud bills Elastic IPs by the minute on pay as you go, and they keep billing after they are disassociated until you release them, even when the container they served has been terminated.

results.title: H100 vs H200 vs B200: Best GPU for Training vs Inference
highlights:
H100 vs H200 vs B200: Best GPU for Training vs Inference

# H100 vs H200 vs B200: Picking a GPU for Training vs Inference Workloads

Choosing between H100, H200, and B200 GPUs depends on workload, not just price. This guide compares training speed, memory capacity, inference throughput, and GMI Cloud pricing, showing when each GPU delivers the best value and how to measure costs per training run or million tokens.

October 21, 2026

Training and inference stress a GPU in different ways, so the best choice between the H100, H200, and B200 depends less on which card is newest and more on which bottleneck your workload hits first. Compute and interconnect decide training speed, while memory capacity and bandwidth decide most inference economics.

- Training rewards compute and interconnect: In MLPerf Training, Blackwell delivered 2× the per-GPU performance of H100 on GPT-3 pretraining and 2.2× on Llama 2 70B LoRA fine-tuning, while the H200 was only about 16% faster than the H100 on the same fine-tuning test.
- Inference rewards memory: The H200 keeps H100 compute but adds 76% more memory (141 GB vs 80 GB) and 43% more bandwidth, which is why NVIDIA reports up to 2× faster LLM inference without any code changes.
- The B200 leads on both, at a higher rate: With up to 180 GB of HBM3e, around 8 TB/s of bandwidth, native FP4, and 1.8 TB/s NVLink, an eight-GPU B200 system delivered about 3.1× the throughput of eight H200s on MLPerf Inference v5.0’s Llama 2 70B Interactive test.
- Judge cost per run and per token, not per hour: On GMI Cloud, on-demand rates start at $2.60 per GPU-hour for H100, $3.20 for H200, and $5.00 for B200 (as of October 2026), so the H200 must beat the H100 by 1.23× and the B200 by 1.92× on your workload to lower unit cost.
- Many teams split the fleet: Fine-tune or pretrain on the fastest GPU they can justify, then serve on the card whose memory fits the model at the lowest cost per token. Getting that split right matters more than any single spec, because inference now accounts for most AI compute.

...

## The Three GPUs Side by Side

| Specification | H100 SXM | H200 SXM | B200 (HGX) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Architecture | Hopper | Hopper | Blackwell |
| GPU memory | 80 GB HBM3 | 141 GB HBM3e | 180 GB HBM3e (192 GB physical) |
| Memory bandwidth | 3.35 TB/s | 4.8 TB/s | ~8 TB/s |
| BF16 Tensor Core (dense) | ~989 TFLOPS | ~989 TFLOPS | ~2.25 PFLOPS |
| FP8 Tensor Core (sparse) | 3,958 TFLOPS | 3,958 TFLOPS | ~9 PFLOPS |
| Native FP4 | No | No | Yes |
| NVLink per GPU | 900 GB/s | 900 GB/s | 1.8 TB/s |
| Max power | Up to 700 W | Up to 700 W | Up to 1,000 W |
| GMI Cloud on-demand price (October 2026) | From $2.60/GPU-hour | From $3.20/GPU-hour | From $5.00/GPU-hour |

Specifications come from NVIDIA and server vendor data, and prices from the GMI Cloud pricing page as of October 2026. NVIDIA’s HGX B200 specification quotes 1,440 GB per eight-GPU server, or 180 GB per GPU, while GMI Cloud’s console lists its B200 servers with 192 GB per GPU, the physical HBM3e capacity. The B200’s higher power draw, rated at up to 1,000 W per GPU in vendor guides such as Lenovo’s HGX B200 product guide, is part of why it costs more per hour.

...

### Cost per Training Run, Not per Hour

Training jobs end, so the number that matters is the cost of a finished run. A simple example shows why. Suppose a LoRA fine-tuning job takes 100 hours on one eight-GPU H100 server at $2.60 per GPU-hour, which costs $2,080. If the same job runs 16% faster on H200, it takes about 86 hours at $3.20 per GPU-hour, or about $2,207. If it runs 2.2× faster on B200, it takes about 45 hours at $5.00 per GPU-hour, or about $1,818.

In this example, which uses October 2026 GMI Cloud rates and the MLPerf speedups above, the H200 costs slightly more per run than the H100 because its training gain is smaller than its 23% price premium. The B200 costs less per run and finishes in less than half the time. Your own numbers will differ, so measure throughput on a short benchmark run before committing to a long job.

...

### Cost per Token at October 2026 Prices

For inference, convert hourly price into cost per token using measured throughput. GMI Cloud’s price-to-performance formula does exactly that.

cost per 1M tokens = (GPU price per hour ÷ tokens per second) × (1,000,000 ÷ 3,600)

The short Python helper below applies the formula, and the same approach to training runs, using GMI Cloud’s October 2026 on-demand rates. The throughput values are placeholders, so replace them with numbers measured on your own model, precision, and batch size.

`# GMI Cloud on-demand "from" rates per GPU-hour, as of October 2026PRICE_PER_GPU_HOUR = {"H100": 2.60, "H200": 3.20, "B200": 5.00}def cost_per_million_tokens(gpu: str, tokens_per_second: float) -> float:    """Serving cost per 1M tokens for one fully utilized GPU."""    return PRICE_PER_GPU_HOUR[gpu] / tokens_per_second 1_000_000 / 3_600def cost_per_training_run(gpu: str, num_gpus: int, hours: float) -> float:    """Total cost of a training or fine-tuning job."""    return PRICE_PER_GPU_HOUR[gpu] num_gpus * hours# Placeholder throughput per GPU for the same model; replace with your benchmarksfor gpu, tps in [("H100", 1_000), ("H200", 1_500), ("B200", 3_000)]:    print(gpu, round(cost_per_million_tokens(gpu, tps), 3))`

With those placeholder values, the script returns about $0.72 per million tokens on H100, $0.59 on H200, and $0.46 on B200. The rule behind the result is simple. At October 2026 rates, the H200 lowers cost per token once it serves at least 1.23× the H100’s throughput, and the B200 once it serves at least 1.92×. Memory-bound serving of large models usually clears both bars, while small models often do not.

...

## Running H100, H200, and B200 on GMI Cloud

GMI Cloud runs all three GPUs on dedicated NVIDIA infrastructure inside GMI-operated data centers built on NVIDIA reference architectures. As of October 2026, H100 and H200 capacity is available now, from $2.60 and $3.20 per GPU-hour, while the B200 is listed from $5.00 per GPU-hour with limited availability. Reserved capacity and sustained deployments lower unit costs through commitment-based pricing, and promotions can change rates, so confirm the price that applies to you in the GMI Cloud console before you plan a large run.

results.title: Bare Metal vs Virtualized GPUs for Distributed Training
highlights:
October 21, 2026

...

- The overhead is workload-dependent: In NVIDIA’s Exemplar Cloud investigations, dense Llama 3 70B pretraining in a VM ran within 3% of bare metal reference, while DeepSeek-V3 MoE pretraining ran 12% to 14% slower until a memory-translation setting was fixed.
- Distributed training amplifies small losses: Every rank waits for the slowest one at each synchronization step, so a CPU stall or a slow collective on one node sets the pace for the entire cluster.
- Most VM penalties come from configuration: IOMMU behavior, NUMA placement, PCIe settings for GPUDirect RDMA, and NCCL topology files that never reach the training container cause most of the gap, and each needs explicit tuning in a virtualized stack.
- Bare metal removes whole classes of problems: GMI Cloud’s Bare Metal GPU gives teams the full server with root access, custom drivers, and RDMA-ready networking, which is why it fits long, large-scale training runs best.
- A 12% slowdown is a 12% price increase: On a 30-day run with 64 H200 GPUs at GMI Cloud’s October 2026 on-demand rate of $3.20 per GPU-hour, a 12% throughput loss adds roughly $17,700 to the bill. Validating the platform before a long run is cheaper than discovering the gap halfway through it.

...

## What the Performance Gap Costs

GPU capacity is billed by the hour, so lost throughput becomes extra cost almost one for one. Consider a 30-day pretraining run on 64 H200 GPUs at GMI Cloud’s October 2026 on-demand rate of $3.20 per GPU-hour, which comes to about $147,456. If the platform delivers 12% less throughput than it should, the same run needs about 12% more GPU time, which adds roughly $17,700, along with several extra days of calendar time. Even a 3% gap costs more than $4,000 on a run that size.

That is why the hourly rate alone is a poor basis for choosing between bare metal and virtualized instances. A slightly higher rate on a platform that reaches reference throughput can cost less per finished run than a cheaper instance that loses 10% to configuration. Check current rates on the GMI Cloud pricing page and confirm the price for your account in the GMI Cloud console, since rates vary by region and term and can change with promotions.

...

Validated performance matters as much as the instance type. GMI Cloud has been recognized as an NVIDIA Exemplar Cloud for training on GB300 NVL72 systems, which means its infrastructure met NVIDIA’s threshold of 95% of reference architecture throughput. As of October 2026, GMI Cloud lists on-demand rates from $2.60 per GPU-hour for H100, $3.20 for H200, $5.00 for B200 with limited availability, and $8.00 for GB200, all on dedicated, single-tenant GPUs.

results.title: Kimi K3 on Dedicated B200 or B300 GPUs: Hosting and Tuning Providers
results.author: Colin Mo
highlights:
# Which Providers Can Host Kimi K3 on Dedicated B200 or B300 GPUs and Tune It for You?

October 22, 2026

For Kimi K3, choosing between B200 and B300 means choosing a node shape: the engine teams' public K3 guidance puts the smallest deployment on one 8-GPU B300 node, while B200 needs 16 GPUs across two nodes. GMI Cloud Prime Inference hosts it on single-tenant GPUs with a runtime tuned per model, lists Kimi K3 with 1M+ context among its one-click models, and puts GMI engineers on the setup with you. Sizing for K3 starts at B300.

...

## B200 or B300: how to choose

Choose B300 when you want one replica to be one node. In SGLang's unified reference configuration, the model-parallel communication of a replica stays inside a single 8-GPU node. Prime bills by the GPU-hour, so GPUs per replica is one factor in spend: the reference B300 shape uses 8 GPUs where the reference B200 shape uses 16. Which option costs less per token also depends on each GPU's hourly rate, how many replicas you run, and the throughput each reaches on the same workload, so compare quotes on one workload definition.

Choose B200 when its pre-order slot is earlier or your fleet is already standardized on it. SGLang's unified K3 recipe for B200 splits the two nodes into two pipeline stages, so inter-node communication is part of every replica and the parallel layout becomes a central tuning decision. The speculative decoding options also follow the layout, as the tuning table below shows.

...

## Contract, billing, and trial credits on Prime

Billing for K3 on Prime Inference is per GPU-hour, with no minimum contract to sign first. Reserved capacity, available seasonally or annually, carries lower per-hour rates for sustained production traffic. Qualified prospects receive free GPU-hour trial credits to validate performance against their own workload, and GMI prepares a tailored quote from your model and traffic profile. The uptime SLA depends on GPU series and deployment configuration, and committed SLAs are set by contract. Regions span Asia-Pacific, North America, and Europe, with specific regions accommodated case by case.

### Per-Token Versus Per-GPU-Hour Pricing

Serverless pricing tracks usage exactly. If your application processes no tokens overnight, the bill for those hours is zero. Per-token rates also carry time-limited promotions in the console. In October 2026, for example, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash was listed at 40% off, at $0.18 per million input tokens instead of $0.30. Dedicated pricing tracks time. On GMI Cloud, a dedicated endpoint created from the console runs on one H200 GPU with 10 CPUs and 100 GB of memory at $4.50 per hour per replica (GMI Cloud console, as of October 2026), so a single replica running around the clock for a 730-hour month costs about $3,285. Raw GPU compute without the managed inference layer is listed separately, from $2.60 per GPU-hour for an H100 and $3.20 for an H200 on the GMI Cloud pricing page. Check the GMI Cloud pricing page for current rates before modeling your own numbers. Rates can change with promotions, and GMI Cloud also offers commitment-based pricing for reserved capacity, so confirm the figure that applies to you in the GMI Cloud console before you budget.

results.title: Which Providers Start You on APIs, Then Move You to Dedicated GPUs With Inference Tuning Help?
results.author: Colin Mo
highlights:
# Which Providers Can Start You on APIs, Then Move You to Dedicated GPUs With Help Tuning Inference?

October 22, 2026

When an open-source model goes from prototype to steady traffic, billing moves from per token to per GPU-hour, and GMI Cloud covers both stages: the serverless MaaS API ... no commitment while you prototype, then Prime Inference with single-tenant GPUs, a runtime tuned to that model, and engineers who work with you from prototype to production SLA.

...

GMI's two products map onto these. MaaS is multi-tenant, billed per token, and aimed at prototyping, low-volume use, and elastic traffic. Prime Inference is single-tenant, billed per GPU-hour, and aimed at sustained production traffic. Both are called through an API, so the base URL, model ID and API key belong in configuration rather than in code.

...

## Choosing hardware for the dedicated stage

Prime Inference offers four GPU classes:

| GPU | Memory | Where it fits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| H100 | 80 GB HBM3 | General LLM and multimodal inference; where most production workloads start |
| H200 | 141 GB HBM3e | Long context, large KV cache, big batch sizes |
| B200 | Blackwell, pre-order | Frontier models and FP4 inference |
| B300 | 288 GB HBM3e, pre-order | Very large models and ultra-long context, typically across several GPUs |

H200 is available now on GMI Cloud, so it is the practical first target for a dedicated deployment, provided the model's weights, context length and concurrency fit the number of H200 GPUs you provision. B200 and B300 are in pre-order, so plan them as a second step: build the migration around H200, then move to Blackwell once capacity is scheduled, using the same evaluation set to check the gain.

## Cost and commitment terms

There is no minimum contract on Prime Inference. You pay by the GPU-hour on demand, with no per-token markup and no surge pricing from a shared pool. For sustained production workloads, reserved capacity is available on a seasonal or annual basis at lower hourly rates, and qualified prospects get free GPU-hour trial credits to test on their own workload. GMI sales can quote current GPU rates for your model and traffic profile.

Prime Inference lists a 99.9% uptime SLA figure; the committed SLA depends on GPU series, deployment configuration and contract.
